readings.title: Is remote work working?
readings.text: Five years ago, most offices insisted that great work needed a shared room. Today, that idea is under review. Companies which moved to hybrid schedules report fewer sick days and lower costs; employees save hours of commuting every week, and many say they are more productive at home. However, the picture is not simple. New employees who have never met their teams in person often feel invisible, and creative work — the kind that grows from accidental corridor conversations — seems harder online. Although younger workers usually prefer flexibility, some admit that home offices blur the line between life and work until answering emails at midnight feels normal again. Perhaps the honest answer is that remote work works when the work is remote-shaped: independent, measured by results, written down. For everything else, the corridor still has value.

readings.title: Should AI write our emails?
readings.text: Last quarter, our company quietly enabled an AI assistant for all internal email. The results were measured, and they are worth reporting precisely. Response times improved by roughly a third, and — perhaps surprisingly — politeness increased: messages drafted by the assistant contain fewer blunt openings and more complete sentences. However, two problems are emerging. First, readers are starting to discount the politeness; when everyone sounds courteous, courtesy stops carrying information. Second, and more seriously, responsibility is blurring. When a wrong figure was sent to a client last month, three people said some version of 'the assistant wrote it.' The tool was not to blame, of course — the signature was. My position is therefore narrow but firm: let the assistant draft, but the name at the bottom owns every word. We are testing a one-line disclosure at the end of assisted emails, and if trust metrics hold, we will keep it. If they do not, we will rethink — in our own words.

readings.title: Quarter in brief: the coffee market
readings.text: Summary for internal circulation — Q3. Prices rose considerably in the first half of the quarter, driven by weather rather than demand: the frost in July affected the two largest producing regions, which together account for roughly 55% of exports. Demand, by contrast, was flat. Supermarket own-brand lines were the least affected, arguably because their contracts are fixed annually; speciality roasters, which buy on the spot market, reported increases of up to forty per cent. It is widely believed that small cafés absorb such increases poorly, and our survey offers some support: 62% said they would rather reduce opening hours than raise the price of an espresso. Looking ahead, futures suggest a partial correction by December, although this depends on rainfall in August. We therefore recommend hedging half of Q4 volume now and reviewing the remainder in October. As ever, this report is a snapshot, not a guarantee.

readings.title: Op-ed: the fifteen-minute fantasy
readings.text: The fifteen-minute city is, depending on who you ask, the future of urban life or a conspiracy with better branding. Strip away the noise, however, and the concept is almost disappointingly modest: housing, work, school and groceries within a short walk. That this modesty has been received as tyranny says less about urbanism than about the era in which it landed. Critics are right about one thing, though — proximity is a luxury good. The neighbourhoods that already deliver it are the most expensive in every city that measures, and a plan that paints a café on a map does not lower the rent. Arguably, then, the real fifteen-minute policy is not zoning but housing: build where people want to live, and the walk to the bakery takes care of itself. None of this makes the idea wrong. It makes it insufficient — which, in a field allergic to nuance, is already an unpopular position.

readings.title: Internal memo: hybrid policy review
readings.text: MEMO — For internal circulation. Re: Hybrid working policy, phase two review. 1. Purpose. This memo summarises the findings of the phase-two review and sets out recommendations for the coming financial year. 2. Findings. Office attendance has averaged 2.3 days per week against a target of three, a shortfall attributable primarily to Wednesdays, which function in practice as a de facto remote day. Cross-team collaboration, as measured by shared project hours, has declined 12% year on year; within-team collaboration is unchanged. Exit interviews cite flexibility as the single most valued benefit (cited by 71% of leavers, compared with 34% for compensation). 3. Recommendations. It is recommended that: (a) Wednesday be designated a full on-site day with team-led programming; (b) the target be revised to an average, not a minimum; (c) the policy be reviewed again in twelve months. 4. Caveat. Attendance data was collected via badge swipes and may undercount presence in non-badged areas.

readings.text: The lock wouldn't turn. That was the first sign. My Airbnb host had sent four codes for one door, and none of them worked. It was 30 degrees, my phone had 4% battery, and a man with a dog was watching me from a window. I typed a message to the host: 'I'm outside, the codes don't work.' Three dots. Nothing. Ten minutes later the dog man opened the door downstairs. 'You must be the Tuscany guest,' he said, in perfect English. 'My daughter manages the flat. Come up, have some water.' By the time I got inside, we had laughed about the codes twice, and he had given me two plums from his tree. Some arrivals are better than the photos.

readings.title: Opinion: AI art is still art
readings.text: The argument against AI art is always the same: a machine cannot feel, therefore it cannot create. But this argument proves too much. If feeling is the requirement, then we must also reject photography (the camera does not feel), digital painting (the software does not feel) and, arguably, most commissioned work (the painter does not always feel either). What matters is not the tool but the intention behind it. A person who writes a prompt, curates the output, revises, and presents the result is making choices. Those choices may be good or bad — that is a separate question. But they are choices, and choices are the raw material of art. The real threat is not AI art; it is the flood of mediocre AI art that drowns the genuinely interesting work. The solution is curation, not prohibition.

readings.title: Policy report: libraries in the digital age
readings.text: 1. Scope. This report examines the role of public libraries in municipalities with populations exceeding 50,000, drawing on data from 340 institutions across 12 countries collected between 2022 and 2025. 2. Principal findings. Contrary to widespread assumptions, circulation of physical books has declined by only 8% since 2022, while attendance at non-book events (workshops, language exchanges, coding clubs) has increased by 210% over the same period. Libraries that rebranded as 'community hubs' saw a 34% increase in first-time visitors; those that maintained a traditional focus saw a 14% decrease. It should be noted, however, that the rebranding group also received 40% more funding on average, making causality difficult to establish. 3. Limitations. The data excludes rural libraries and does not distinguish between scheduled and walk-in attendance. 4. Recommendation. Municipalities should fund libraries as social infrastructure rather than as book warehouses, and should commission a follow-up study with better attendance methodology.

readings.text: How does a design studio of twelve people ship so much work? 'We don't do everything ourselves — we get it done,' says Marta Rubio, who runs a small studio in Valencia. Her rule is simple: any task that a specialist can do faster goes out. The studio has its accounts managed by an external firm, its website maintained by a freelancer and its meeting rooms cleaned every evening. 'I used to put off the boring jobs,' Rubio admits. 'Now I set up a rota, follow up once a week and let other people carry out the rest.' Not everyone agrees that outsourcing is always cheaper, however. A consultant who studied small firms found that managers who delegate everything often lose touch with the details. Her advice is to keep the work that teaches you something and to pay for the rest. That balance, she argues, is the real skill — the chores you give away buy the hours you think in.

readings.title: The science of the what-if
readings.text: Why do we replay our mistakes for years? Psychologists who study regret say it is surprisingly useful. In one study, travellers who had missed a train felt worse than travellers who had simply arrived late — but they also checked timetables far more carefully afterwards. Regret, the researchers argue, is the brain's way of rewriting the past so that we do things better next time. Interestingly, the most common regrets are not about mistakes but about chances people did not take: the message never sent, the course never started, the trip never planned. 'If only I had tried' lasts longer than 'I wish I hadn't said that', because a closed door explains itself while an open one keeps asking questions. The researchers' advice is simple. When you make a mistake, ask what you would do differently, write it down, and then close the file: a lesson you have written down stops repeating itself, while a regret you keep replaying never ends.

readings.title: Opinion: hype is not a business model
readings.text: Every technology wave produces the same headline: a start-up is rumoured to be 'in talks', and its valuation doubles overnight. It is worth asking what a rumour is actually worth. The answer, in my view, is nothing — or worse, because rumour is a currency that only spends in one direction. When it is reported that a young company has signed a major client, early investors celebrate; when the report turns out to be premature, nobody is held to account. An industry that prices what is whispered rather than what is verified will eventually treat fiction as fact. The defenders of hype reply that optimism is fuel: without belief, nothing gets built. True — but it proves too little. Belief belongs to the founders who ship; speculation belongs to the markets, and the two must not be confused. The discipline I would like to see is simple: no valuation before verification. A start-up that is genuinely likely to change a market does not need the rumour mill, because the evidence will do the job faster. Until then, read every 'is believed to' as 'somebody hopes' — and price it accordingly.
